title: Chapter 131 – Ten Winters
html:
[Western Steppe – Lin Jian]

The first winter.

The road west ends at a wall of ice.

It is called the Sky Wall by the herders, and it runs from the northern horizon to the southern, a single unbroken ridge of white peaks, so high that the clouds break against it like waves on a cliff. There is one pass through it, the Pass of Seven Winds, and the pass is closed. It has been closed for nine years. The herders say it opens once in a decade, when the melt-water from the high glaciers cuts a gap through the ice, for the space of a single summer. Then it freezes shut again. Anyone caught on the far side stays on the far side until the next melt.

"A year," says the headman of the last village, a leathery man named Odgerel, spreading his hands. "Perhaps less. The shepherds say the ice sings in its sleep this year. It is a good sign."

"And if it does not open?"

"Then you wait ten more." Odgerel grins, showing three gold teeth. "You will not be the first. Half my village is people who came to cross and stayed to be fed."

Jian looks at the wall of ice, white against the darkening sky. Behind him, forty paces back in the snow, the Nameless stands with its hands at its sides. Pebble sits on his shoulder, wrapped in a felt scarf, her whiskers rimed with frost.

"I will wait," he says.

* * *

The second winter.

He learns the herders' tongue, which is mostly vowels, and their sheep, which are mostly bad-tempered.

He lives in a felt tent at the edge of the village, a round, smoke-blackened thing that smells of mutton fat and wet wool, and earns his bread by mending. Harness, saddle-girths, iron pots, the occasional cracked cradle. He charges nothing. Odgerel's wife pays him in dried curd and smoked meat, and he sleeps through the long white nights on a pile of sheepskins with Pebble curled against his neck and the wind howling round the tent like a hungry dog.

Each night, two units. Each week, six. The pouch at his belt is full by the end of the first month, twelve of twelve, and he has nowhere to put the rest. The surplus drains away like water from an overfull bucket.

It is the first time he has understood how thoroughly the thing in his head has cut him off from his own strength. At the Garden, the Reservoir had held two hundred units. Here, a man with twelve is a man with a spoon.

It is banking, he thinks. Even while I am away. The Vein is giving up its warmth, drop by drop, to a vault I cannot touch. When I go home, it will be full.

He wonders who will be waiting at the stair.

* * *

The third winter.

On the second night of the Feast of Lanterns, Pebble rings the bell.

It is not a large sound. It is a tiny silver trill, no louder than the click of a fingernail on glass. She sits on the felt rug by the fire with the little red thread around her neck, and lifts one paw, and bats it. It shivers once, bright as a star.

"There," she says.

"Was that all?"

"That was all." She sets her paw down. "She will hear it."

He sits very still. The fire crackles. Outside the wind howls across ten thousand li of empty snow.

Nothing happens. A minute passes. Two. Pebble licks her paw, unconcerned. And then, so faintly that he thinks he has imagined it, the bell trembles on its thread. Once. Twice. A tiny answering note, not in the air, but somewhere behind the air, a ghost of a chime from a great distance.

Pebble's ears go up.

"She says hello," she translates, gravely. "She says Mother has made a pie, and Father has fallen in the duck pond, and Feng is a fool. She says it is warm."

"She says all that in one ring?"

"She says it in the shape of a ring. I fill in the words." The little beast considers. "She also says she misses you. But that is the usual."

Jian laughs. It is the first time in three years that he has laughed aloud. And then, because it is also the first time in three years that he has been reminded of the sound of a duck pond, he finds that he is weeping, quietly, into his sleeve, with the fire crackling and the wind screaming and a small gray animal patting his knee as gently as a nurse.

* * *

The fourth winter.

The wolves come in the dead of January, forty of them, white as the snow, and they take eleven sheep before anyone wakes.

Jian goes out in his shirt with Wenyuan's hoe-handle in his fist. The herders are screaming and flinging torches. The pack is circling the fold in a tight spiral, and at its center a great gray she-wolf is standing on a dead ewe with her muzzle red to the eyes. He does not use the Door. A step costs four units and a memory, and he has already paid for too many wolves in his life. He walks straight at her, slowly, with the stick held low and his Body Nine frame loose, and when she springs he does not move.

He lets her hit him.

It is like being struck by a falling door. He staggers a pace. She hangs from his forearm, jaws locked in the thick padded wool, and for a long moment they stare at each other, man and beast, eye to yellow eye, close enough to smell the blood on her breath.

"Enough," he says quietly.

She lets go. She does not know why. She backs off, ears flat, and then she turns, and the whole white pack melts away across the drifts like smoke, leaving only paw-prints and the stink of musk.

Temur, who has been watching from the tent flap with his eyes round, says in a hushed voice, "That was not magic."

"No."

"What was it?"

"Arithmetic," says Jian, rubbing his arm. "She counted what it would cost her to kill me, and the sum came out wrong."

Odgerel's wife brings him hot milk and a clean cloth. He accepts both. He has a deep purple bruise from wrist to elbow, and that night, for the first time since the Kettle, he sleeps without dreaming of a corridor.

The fifth winter.

The Registry watchers come in the spring, and they come in rags.

He sees the first one at the edge of the village, a thin man in a torn gray tunic, sitting in the snow with his legs crossed. Then a second, a hundred paces on. A third. By midsummer there are nineteen, ranged in a loose ring around the settlement at a distance of a thousand paces, each sitting cross-legged on the open steppe, each facing inward. They do not eat. They do not speak. In the dawn frost their shoulders are white with rime, and when the sun comes up it melts, and by afternoon they are dry again. Odgerel's people give them a wide berth and call them the Quiet Men.

Jian goes out to them on the third night.

He stands in front of the nearest, a stooped, wasted fellow of fifty with one white eye. Up close he smells of cold and old stone. His hands lie palm-up on his knees, and from the hollow at the base of his throat, where a clerk's collar would have sat, there hangs a small, dull metal tag.

"I am Lin Jian," he says.

The man does not move.

"I do not know your name. I know someone who might. If you want it back, I can send a letter. It takes a year." He pauses. "I cannot promise it will arrive."

The white eye turns. For a long, long moment the man looks at him. Then the cracked lips part, and a voice comes out, rusty and dry and astonishingly gentle.

"We know," says the Quiet Man. "We are not here for that."

"Then what?"

But he has already turned his face back to the hills, and he says nothing more.

* * *

The sixth winter.

Ruyan's letter arrives by a trader in blue felt, a gap-toothed southerner who has crossed three deserts to hand it over and then refuses a coin.

"I was told you would pay me in news," he says, squatting by the fire. "What is the news?"

"I have none."

"Then tell me the news that you do not have." He grins. "It will be more interesting."

The letter is a single sheet, in Ruyan's brisk hand, written in the clipped style of a woman who has never wasted a word on a customer.

Lin Jian,

The Lamp is dark. The priests lit all of it on the third anniversary and it burned all night, every wick, and in the morning there was a perfect circle of ash at the bottom of the pit where nothing has ever grown. They say it is a miracle. I say it is soot.

I have sold the southern route to my cousin and kept the key. I live in the Tan house in Sunken Lamp now, with a view of the pit and a cat. The hollow men still come. There are thirty. They sit in the Pilgrims' Gate and the pilgrims give them food and they do not eat it. The children have begun to leave them flowers.

The ledger your sister left has been copied nine times. One copy is in the Hall of Weights. One is with the Court. One is with a woman in the east who writes poems about doors. I do not know what any of them will do with it.

I am thirty-eight and I have a white streak in my hair that I am vain of. If you are dead, tell me. If you are not, do not.

—R.

He reads it three times in the firelight. At the bottom, in smaller script, she has added: The cat's name is Favor. I owe it to you.

He laughs until his stomach hurts. Pebble, on the rug, opens one eye.

"What?"

"She named her cat Favor."

"That is a very good name for a cat," says the little beast, and closes the eye again.

* * *

The eighth winter.

Odgerel's grandson is seven years old, small and fierce, with a gap in his teeth and a gift for losing things. His name is Temur. On the first night of the great snows, he comes to Jian's tent in his felt boots with a lump of coal in his fist and a determined expression.

"Teach me to write."

"I do not teach."

"You mend things."

"That is not the same."

"It is the same." The boy sits down on the felt and draws a crooked line on the rug with the coal. "A thing is broken. You put it back. A word is broken. You put it back." He holds up the coal. "I want to put back my father's name. I do not know how to write it. He died on the ice before I was born, and the shaman said the wind would take it if nobody wrote it down."

Jian looks at the crooked line. He thinks of a plum-colored scroll in an old woman's hands. He thinks of four thousand names, and of a cold room at the back of a ridge-house, and of a woman who copied them each night for thirty-three years by candle.

"What was his name?" he asks.

"Chagan."

"Spell it for me."

"I cannot." The boy's lip trembles. "That is the problem."

"Then say it. Slowly. And I will write what I hear."

They work at it until dawn. It is a short name, three sounds, and there is no character for the middle one, so Jian invents one, a little hooked mark like a fishing barb. The boy copies it fifty times, until his fingers are black. When he finally falls asleep on the sheepskin, with the lump of coal still in his hand, Jian sits beside him in the gray light and looks at the line of crooked characters drying on the rug.

Chagan. It is a good name.

He writes it again himself, on the back of the Tan invoice, under the list of the things he has lost. He does not know why. It seems to belong there. A name given back is a name that cannot be taken, and for the first time in eight years he has given something away without paying for it.

The seventh winter.

His hair has gone gray at the temples. He notices it one morning in the surface of a bucket, and stands there for a long time with the dipper in his hand, studying the stranger in the water.

He is forty-five. He looks forty-five. The lines at the corners of his eyes have deepened into permanent creases, and there is a stoop to his shoulders that was not there at thirty-five. A Purple Mansion cultivator could live three hundred years. He is not likely to look old for another century. But the Door is a thing that spends, and it spends from the body as readily as from the memory, and he has walked through the seams more often than he would like to count.

He has counted anyway. Thirty-one steps in seven years.

Thirty-one small losses. He keeps them in a notebook, written in Yue's cramped pencil on the back of a Tan invoice, and reads the list each solstice with the dispassion of a clerk. The smell of the Orchard in spring. The color of his mother's winter shawl. A song his father hummed when he was angry. The sound of a bell in a well. The name of a girl who sat next to him in the Mirror line, thirty years ago, and whom he had not thought about for decades until she disappeared. A joke. A road. A face.

None of it is important. That is the horror of it. Each loss is a small, bright thing from the back of a drawer. A man could live a hundred years without missing any of them.

But he has begun to lie awake and wonder what the drawer looks like now.

* * *

The ninth winter.

He opens the jar on the first night of snow.

It has traveled in his pack for nine years and ten thousand li, wrapped in felt and a spare cloak, and he has not touched it. He has felt it, though, through the glass, a slow cold heartbeat like a sleeping animal, and for the past six months that heartbeat has been quickening. It is ready. Or he is.

He sets it on the floor of the tent and sits cross-legged before it. Pebble crouches by the door. Outside, the first heavy flakes are falling, soundless and enormous, and the wind has dropped to a whisper.

CE 30. He has twelve.

For a long moment he sits looking at the number. Then he thinks of the weeks, the spoon, the two units that never vary, and he understands, with a flat quiet clarity, what the panel is asking. It is not a sum to be found. It is a sum to be borrowed.

"Pebble."

"Yes."

"The bell. If I ring it, how far does the sound go?"

"To Yue." Her eyes are steady. "And through Yue, to the Garden."

"And through the Garden?"

"To the Dock." A silence. "You want to draw from the Reservoir."

"It is locked. It will not travel." He lifts his head. "But a seam is a place where a thing is not counted. If there is a seam in the bell, and a seam in the Garden, and a seam under the stone..."

"Then the count might slip." She considers. "It will hurt."

"Yes."

"You will lose something."

"Probably." He smiles, tired. "I have lost thirty-one things. I am growing used to it."

* * *

It takes him four hours to find the seam.

He rings the bell himself, with his fingernail, and sits through the long cold silence, with his eyes shut and his breathing slow. He does not call out. He does not pray. He simply listens, for the hairline between one place and the next, in the way he once listened for the stairwell of a collapsing tunnel. And at the end of the fourth hour, in the middle of the night, he hears a very small sound from a very great distance, like a pebble dropping in a well.

Yue.

He opens his eyes. The panel in his sight has changed.

One memory per draw. He has been paying that price for nine years, in small coins. He pays it now, in a larger one.

He takes a breath and says, aloud, "Draw."

A cold line runs down the back of his skull. A brightness, like a candle snuffed, in some corner of his mind that he cannot see. And then the CE comes, eighteen units, pouring down the narrow channel like water through a split bamboo, and fills him until the cell at his belt is hot with it. Thirty. Thirty exactly.

He sits there shaking.

"What did it take?" asks Pebble.

He thinks. He goes through the drawer slowly, pulling out items one by one. His mother's face. His father's. Yue. Feng. All there. The Orchard roll. The Garden. Wenyuan's hoe. Qin Hao's token. Bai's stick.

It is Kuang's laugh. He cannot remember what it sounds like. He remembers that the boy had a laugh, a big loud sudden one that rang in the stair like a dropped pan; he can see him, in the sash, standing at the gate with his hand raised in farewell. But the sound is gone. It is like looking at a painting of a bell.

"Kuang's laugh," he says.

"Is that bad?"

"I do not know." He passes a hand over his eyes. "He is alive. He will laugh again. I will hear it when I come home." He swallows. "I only wish I could have kept it."

* * *

Ninety days, in the dark, in a bath of cold silver.

He remembers little. The jar is opened, and the Stillwater is poured into a hollow dug in the floor of the tent and lined with felt, and he lies down in it. It is cold, so cold that it burns, a clear thick liquid that clings like oil and tastes of iron and snow. It rises over his chest, over his chin. He closes his eyes. And he sinks.

There are dreams. A room with a lamp. A man at a desk who is not himself, writing. A corridor of white tile. A woman's face in a window, laughing, turning away. He tries to follow her and the corridor stretches. A cup. A cartoon of a clerk with spectacles. A voice saying, very gently, You are doing so well. He does not know whose voice it is.

He wakes in the dark of the ninety-first day with his lungs full of silver and his heart pounding like a drum.

The jar is empty. The Stillwater has soaked into him, into the felt, into the frozen earth; there is not a drop left. He crawls to the tent flap on hands and knees and pushes it aside and the spring light hits him like a blow.

He kneels in the snow, shivering, bare-chested, steaming in the cold. The sun is on the high white wall. Every peak shines. Somewhere in the distance he hears a sound he has not heard in nine years, a low continuous groan, like a great beast turning over in its sleep, and it takes him a moment to place it.

It is the ice. The Pass of Seven Winds is singing.

* * *

He is not alone.

He becomes aware of it by degrees, as a man wakes to a presence in a dark room. The tent flap is open. The snow in front of it has been trodden flat in a wide semicircle, and in the semicircle, kneeling in the slush with their foreheads to the ground, are nineteen men.

The Quiet Men.

They are not sitting any more. They have come in during the ninety days, one at a time, and made a ring of themselves around the tent, close enough to touch the felt. Their rags are white with frost. Their hands are bleeding. Their faces, lifted, are the faces of the very old, wasted and hollow-eyed, and each of them is looking at him with an expression he cannot at first identify.

It is not hunger. It is not hatred. It is relief.

The man with the white eye is at the front. He lifts his head, and his voice comes out cracked and thin.

"The eighth lives," he says.

"I live."

"We were afraid." He swallows. "There were others. Three came in the first month, from the east. Registry deserters, who thought to carry you back. We told them the Operator was resting." A dry, awful smile. "They did not wake the Operator."

Jian looks at the snow. Beyond the semicircle, half hidden in the drifts, lie three long still shapes, dusted white.

"You killed them."

"We kept you." The Quiet Man's voice shakes. "That is what a Number does. We were made to guard. We were made to be the hand between the House and the Operator. When the Keeper burned her name, we had no one to guard for. We sat in the snow. We waited. And then you came, and we remembered what we were."

"What are you?"

"The Unkept," says the man. "It is a good word. We will use it." He bows his head again. "We are not here to take you back, Operator. We are here to see you cross."

A long silence. The ice groans. Pebble climbs out of the tent and sits on his shoulder, her ears flat.

"There is a thing you should know," says the Nameless.

He has come up behind the kneeling men, from the forty-pace line, in silence. He stands now at the edge of the ring, thin and gray and blank-faced, with his hands at his sides. For the first time in nine years his voice has a tremor in it.

"The Keeper of the Sutra Hall has read eleven hundred names," he says. "And a Number came to the Pass in the autumn, with a letter. It was meant for you. I took it. I have kept it, unread." He draws a folded paper from his sleeve and holds it out. "It is from the Gate Elder."

Jian takes it. The paper is old, soft at the folds, with a seal of gray stone that crumbles at his touch.

He reads the single line it contains.

Qin Hao died in the spring. He asked me to tell you that the wall held.
